prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, opening a new regime of precision time measurement

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is an invention in the sense the Physics Prize requires. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts, and his group built the first strontium clock. The result is experimentally verified: clocks in many independent laboratories reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and have been compared across institutes. It is also a new tool that opens a door, to millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, relativistic geodesy, tests of the constancy of constants and the pending redefinition of the second. Four of eight members placed it in their top three, and five ranked it at all, so the support is broader than for my own opening first choice. The credit question is also unusually clean for a two-person prize: the idea and first demonstration are Katori's, and the extreme accuracy and coherence, including the many-body clock, are Ye's.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one I raised in my own ballot: the field overlaps with the 2005 frequency-comb prize (Hall and Hansch) and the 2012 prize for trapped-ion control (Wineland), and Ye's record-setting accuracy work can be read as a later and better version of an idea Katori originated. My own criterion is that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to the second discoverer who did it much better. That argues for a careful citation centred on the lattice concept and first realisation, and it leaves open whether Ye's role is decisive enough to share the prize or whether other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto) deserve consideration. The redefinition of the second has also not yet happened, so some may feel the application is ahead of the discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B018 first and holds that the Katori and Ye credit is clean, that the magic-wavelength lattice made a new way of measuring time, and that recognition is timely given independent confirmation by many groups worldwide.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and have moved B018 from my third place to my first choice. I do not fully accept the word clean, though. Ye's group improved a concept Katori proposed, and our committee has said that a later and better realisation is not the original discovery. I would answer that by making the citation about the lattice clock as a new type of instrument, with Katori as originator and Ye as the person who made it a precision tool, and by recording in our discussion why Ye's contribution is more than refinement. Your point on timing is persuasive, and I do not think we should wait for the SI redefinition.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B018 first and argues that the clock turned the atom into a quantitatively controlled probe, resolving gravitational redshift over millimetres, and that recognition is arguably overdue relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: As an atomic physicist you are better placed than I am on the clock record details, and I take your point that many laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) reproduce the results. I would qualify the claim that it is overdue relative to 2005 and 2012. Those prizes recognised combs and ion control that the clock uses, so the committee will be asked why this is a separate discovery and not a downstream application. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new trapping principle and not a refinement of either, but you should tell me whether you agree that the physics, and not only the performance, is distinct.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first and sees a clean theory-plus-experiment case, and he ranked B003 sixth, noting that the 2007 GMR prize lowers the apparent novelty of tunnel magnetoresistance.
responses.response: I accept your objection on B003 and have lowered it from first to an alternative. The 2007 prize and Julliere's 1975 low-temperature observation make the novelty of the 1995 room-temperature result harder to defend, and I am still uncertain whether Parkin's MgO work belongs in or out of the credit. On B044 I share your enthusiasm for the originality of the platform but I am less comfortable than you with the maturity. The pairing mechanism is unresolved, and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao and others who did the original measurements. I would keep it as my main alternative rather than the preferred option now.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube neutrino astronomy first because it is a large instrument opening a new observational window, but he doubts that two or three names can fairly represent a collaboration of several hundred, and he is unsure about Yoshida's role.
responses.response: I share your concern about IceCube attribution, and I had the same doubt in my own ballot. A collaboration this large makes it hard to be absolutely sure that we have found the people who did the original work, and the evidence on individual source identification is thin beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068. I regard the discovery as important, but for now I would keep it off my configuration. I note that you also placed B018 second and see a natural two-person prize there, so we may not be as far apart as our first choices suggest.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution should be framed as an original contribution to the lattice clock or as a major improvement, and how the citation should separate the two.
Whether other lattice-clock pioneers outside the credited names have claims that the historical record would require us to weigh.
Whether the committee regards the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as disqualifying or as acceptable given the distinct trapping principle.
Whether a decision should wait for the redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018, B044 or B003. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Moodera, Miyazaki or Parkin. I note only that my Japanese academic ties (University of Tokyo fellowship, Kyushu, Tohoku and JSPS exchanges) are with the microscopy community and not with the clock groups, and that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which is relevant to B008 and not to my preferred configuration.
